opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a fairly intuitive relationship, though I'd frame it as an empirical tendency rather than a law.

As models get larger, they tend to tolerate more attention sparsity. Part of the reason is redundancy. A big model has many layers and many heads, and a lot of the information each token needs is represented in more than one place. If one attention pattern skips some tokens, other heads or later layers can often recover what was lost. A small model doesn't have that slack. Every head is doing heavy lifting, so when you sparsify its attention, you're more likely to cut something it actually needed.

The second reason is that larger models seem to learn sharper attention. When you look at the attention distributions, a lot of the probability mass concentrates on a small number of tokens: some local context, a few semantically key positions, sometimes "sink" tokens at the start. If the true distribution is already effectively sparse, a sparse mechanism that picks the right top-k tokens loses very little. Smaller models often have flatter, more diffuse attention, so truncating it hurts more.

But I'd add two caveats.

First, "tolerate" depends heavily on how the sparsity is introduced. If you take a dense model and sparsify it after training, you see one picture. If you train with a sparse or learned-selection mechanism from the start, or at least do substantial continued training with it, the model adapts its representations to the constraint. Then the gap between sparse and dense can be much smaller, even at moderate scale. So a lot of what looks like a capacity limit is really a mismatch between how the model was trained and how it's run.

Second, the task matters as much as the size. For short-context benchmarks almost anything works. The real test is long-context retrieval and multi-step reasoning, where the model has to find one specific piece of information buried far back and use it precisely. That's where poorly designed sparsity breaks first, regardless of scale. So I care less about a single sparsity ratio and more about whether the selection mechanism can reliably find the tokens that matter.

My overall view is that scale gives you more headroom for sparsity. But the bigger lever is making sparsity something the model learns end to end, rather than a heuristic bolted on afterward. Once the model decides for itself where to look, sparsity becomes much less of a compromise and more of a natural fit for how attention already behaves.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says larger models tend to tolerate more attention sparsity than smaller models, describing scale as giving more headroom for sparsity.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that bigger models tolerate much more sparsity than people intuitively expect, and the reason is less about the attention mechanism itself and more about where the information actually lives.

Let me explain what I mean. When you look at the attention patterns in a large model, most heads, most of the time, are attending to a very small number of tokens. The attention weights are already extremely peaked. So in a sense, dense attention is doing a lot of work to compute scores that end up being nearly zero anyway. Sparsity is not really removing information, it is removing the computation that was proving the information wasn't there. The question is just how well you can predict in advance which tokens matter.

And that prediction gets easier as the model gets bigger, for a couple of reasons. First, a larger model has more heads and more layers, so there is redundancy. If one head misses something because of the sparse selection, another head or a later layer usually recovers it. A small model doesn't have that slack. Every head is carrying a heavier load, so when you cut its context, you feel it immediately in the loss. Second, larger models tend to have cleaner, more specialized attention behavior. Retrieval heads become very obvious, local heads become very obvious, and that structure is exactly what a sparse scheme exploits. In small models, the roles are more mixed, so a fixed sparse pattern cuts across things it shouldn't.

There is also a representational argument. In a big model, the hidden state at each position is already a pretty good summary of what came before. So when you do something like block selection or a learned indexer that picks the top-k blocks, the summary vectors you are scoring against are informative enough that top-k actually captures what you need. In a small model, those summaries are weaker, so the selection is noisier, and noisy selection compounds across layers.

So the practical rule we found is something like: the sparsity ratio you can afford grows with scale, and it is not a small effect. At small scale you might only safely drop half the keys. At the scale of a frontier model you can go down to a small percentage of the context being attended to per query and the loss curve is almost on top of the dense baseline, sometimes even slightly better because you are removing a little noise.

But I want to add two caveats, because I think people over-generalize this. One is that it depends a lot on whether the sparsity is trained in from the start or bolted on afterwards. If you train with a sparse mechanism natively, the model learns to put information where the selector will find it. If you take a dense model and sparsify it post hoc, the tolerance is much lower at every scale, because the model had no reason to organize itself that way. The second is that tolerance is task-dependent. Average perplexity hides a lot. Long-context retrieval, multi-hop reasoning over a long document, those stress the selection mechanism specifically, and a big model that looks fine on perplexity can still show degradation there. So when we evaluate sparsity at scale, I always want to see the needle-type benchmarks and the reasoning benchmarks separately, not just the loss.

If I had to compress it into one sentence: scale buys you redundancy and better summaries, and both of those are exactly what sparse attention needs in order not to hurt. That's why I'm fairly optimistic that for the very large models, near-linear attention cost is achievable without giving up much, while for small models I'd be more careful.

r001.rationale: The response says larger models tolerate “much more sparsity” and contrasts this with smaller models, which feel context cuts more immediately.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that attention sparsity and model size have to be considered together. By tolerating sparsity, I mean how much attention computation we can remove while maintaining roughly the same model quality.

A larger model may have more redundancy and more capacity to compensate for sparse attention, so it can potentially tolerate a higher sparsity ratio. But I wouldn’t treat that as a universal rule. Adding parameters doesn’t automatically make the information you remove less important. Where you apply sparsity, which tokens remain visible, and whether the model was trained with that pattern all matter.

So I’d look at a quality–compute curve for each model size, rather than assume one sparsity ratio works everywhere. The practical question is: at a fixed compute budget, does a larger, sparser model outperform a smaller, denser one? And that needs to be measured under comparable training conditions and on tasks that actually require the context you’re making sparse.

r001.rationale: The response says larger models may have more redundancy and capacity to compensate, so they can potentially tolerate a higher sparsity ratio.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that model size and attention sparsity shouldn’t be considered independently. A larger model may have more redundancy across its attention heads and layers, so it can potentially tolerate more sparsity. But that doesn’t mean you can simply increase the sparsity ratio as you increase the parameter count and expect the same quality.

What matters is which attention connections you retain. If you preserve the connections carrying important information, you can remove a substantial amount of computation. If you remove those critical connections, even a very large model can fail. And the tolerance will differ across layers, heads, and tasks—especially when a task requires retrieving specific information from a long context.

So I would treat model size as one factor, rather than a direct rule for choosing sparsity. The practical question is: for a particular model and workload, how much attention computation can we remove while preserving the capabilities we care about?

r001.rationale: The response says larger models may have more redundancy and therefore can potentially tolerate more attention sparsity, conveying the stated comparison.
